title: Kintsugi: Task-Gated Repair Reaches Full-Precision Agent Scores at 2.5 Bits
description: Low-bit quantization of language models is usually tuned on an average error such as KL divergence. The Kintsugi method gates every change and every repair on task probes next to KL, with pass lines written before each run. On two model families, the 12 GB builds that came out of this loop, at about 2.5 bits per coded weight, reach the AppWorld scores of the full-precision weights: on Qwen3.8-27B the shipped build (the published bit allocation with our fits, head and runtime) and the map that the loop repaired; on Inkling 2 Mini our map (596 against 592 of 672). On the 27B model, average KL would have picked lower-scoring maps. Such results sit at single decisions that a benchmark total hides: decision-point habits. We detect one by a turn-type split, replay the deciding call on a frozen history, and locate it by tensor copies between files. (1) Qwen3.8-27B, BFCL: when a held-back tool returns, the model often says the tool is absent although the new tool list is in its prompt. At temperature 0.001 in one setup, BF16 misses 61 of 200 such turns and the 2.47-bit build 36 (p = 1.1e-4). Stripping earlier thinking removes 40-62 % of the build's misses. Tensor copies pointed at the fits of two same-map files on the public entries; on the development half of a fresh private set that gap was not shown, and a graft chosen there was not confirmed on the sealed half. (2) Inkling 2 Mini, a pre-registered confirm on fresh tasks: the first reply that the client receives has no code in 46 % of calls for the official weights, 45 % for a public 2-bit file and 11 % for our map; no task cost is shown. No build was made to change a habit. A map built to remove one, confirmed on held-out turns, is the open step. We did not invent the quantizer, the trellis codec or the 27B bit allocation.
